The Silvertip shark Carcharhinus albimarginatus is a large, pelagic carcharhinid found throughout the tropical Indo-Pacific, often associated with offshore islands and coral drop-offs. Neonates are typically observed in shallow, coastal nursery grounds following parturition, with a total length at birth of approximately 65.5 centimeters [Lb = approximately 65.5 centimeters], though litter surveys have documented a range between 63 and 68 centimeters. This relatively modest birth size, compared to the dimensions attained by mature adults, reflects the species' reliance on a placental viviparous mode of reproduction. The gestation period involves a complex uterine embryogenesis and the age at birth is roughly 19 months [ab = roughly 19 months] at a mean water temperature of 27 °C [T = 27 °C]. This prolonged developmental phase, consistent with that of other large carcharhinids, underscores the high maternal investment required to produce well-developed, free-swimming pups capable of independent foraging onset immediately after the exotrophic transition. Early life stages thus involve a significant time commitment within the uterine environment before neonates enter the pelagic juvenile ecosystem.

As juveniles mature, a pronounced sexual dimorphism in size at puberty becomes apparent. Females reach the onset of reproductive maturity at a total length at puberty of 175 centimeters [Lp = 175 centimeters], whereas males mature at a somewhat smaller total length at puberty of 170 centimeters [Lp = 170 centimeters]. This modest divergence in maturation size is a common pattern among carcharhinid sharks and likely reflects the greater body volume females require to support gestation and yolk provisioning. Reaching these size thresholds requires several years of sustained growth in productive reef and pelagic foraging habitats.

The ultimate body size attained by the Silvertip shark also differs between the sexes. Females grow to an ultimate total length of 300 centimeters [Li = 300 centimeters], while males reach a somewhat smaller ultimate total length of 280 centimeters [Li = 280 centimeters]. Corresponding to the female asymptotic length, the ultimate wet weight of this species reaches approximately 208,700 grams [Wwi = approximately 208,700 grams], a substantial body mass that places the Silvertip shark among the larger reef-associated carcharhinids. This considerable size confers a competitive advantage in prey acquisition, allowing adults to take a broad range of teleosts and cephalopods.

Reproductive output in this species is modest, consistent with a slow, K-selected life history. Under the thermal conditions of its tropical range (22 °C [T = 22 °C]), females produce between one and eleven pups per litter, with a single litter typically produced every two years. This low reproductive frequency, combined with the prolonged nineteen-month gestation, results in a comparatively low lifetime reproductive output that renders the species vulnerable to overfishing. Longevity records indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 25 years [am = approximately 25 years] at the same reference temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], a duration that allows mature females to complete multiple reproductive cycles across their lifetime despite the extended interval between successive litters.
